title: Python and FastAPI, from the basics
blurb: Python and FastAPI for PHP developers: the language, an API, SQLAlchemy and pytest, ready for a live code review in three days.
lede: Python and FastAPI for PHP developers, in three days.

shift.label: The one big mental shift
shift.html:
PHP starts fresh for every request and throws everything away at the end. A Python server is one long-running process that handles thousands of requests. Anything at module level (a variable, a list, a database session) lives across requests and is shared between them.

When you review a snippet, ask: what here is shared that PHP would have thrown away? And what here waits without await?

plan_foot: When you finish a day, ask an AI assistant or a friend for concept-first questions on those topics, and answer out loud.

items.t: Run Python and keep projects apart with a virtualenv
items.why: python3 -m venv .venv, source .venv/bin/activate, pip install httpx. A venv is a per-project vendor/; uv does the same faster. Try lines in the REPL (python3) as you read.
No braces, no semicolons, no $. Blocks start with : and are indented 4 spaces. if / elif / else, for x in items:, while, range(5).
Strings are immutable. Build them with f-strings: f"{name} has {n} items". None is PHP's null; True/False are capitalised.

items.t: PHP's array splits in two: list and dict
items.why: [1, 2, 3] is a list (ordered, by position). {"a": 1} is a dict (by key). Also tuple (fixed, immutable) and set (unique). d["missing"] raises KeyError; d.get("missing") returns None.

items.t: Loops the Python way: enumerate, zip, slicing, comprehensions
items.why: for i, x in enumerate(xs) instead of a counter. xs[1:3], xs[-1]. [u.name for u in users if u.active] replaces most array_map / array_filter.
def send(to, body, *, retries=3): everything after * must be passed by name. Call with send("a", "hi", retries=1). Functions are values; you can pass them around.
Every .py file is a module; a folder of them is a package. from app.models import User is use App\Models\User. if __name__ == "__main__": runs only when the file is run directly.
__init__ is the constructor; self is $this, written out as the first parameter. No private: a leading _ means "internal". @dataclass writes the constructor for plain data classes.
Module-level variables, lists and sessions live across requests and are shared between them. PHP-FPM throws them away after each request. Many bugs come from this one difference.
The default is created once, when the function is defined, and shared by every call. Fix: default to None and create the list inside.
if not token: treats an empty string and None the same. Know when you mean is None. Watch for checks that fail open when config is empty.
is checks identity. Use it only for None, True, False. Everything else uses ==.

items.t: try / except / finally, and why bare except: pass is bad
items.why: Catch the specific exception you expect. A bare except swallows every error, even typos and shutdown signals, so bugs disappear silently.
with open(...) and with Session(engine) as s: close the resource even when an error happens. Like a guaranteed finally.
Always use datetime.now(timezone.utc). Comparing a naive and an aware datetime raises TypeError. Naive times on a server are in whatever zone its clock uses, often hours off.
src: Python docs: aware and naive objects

items.why: Same as PHP hash_equals(). Plain == can leak timing information. A unit test can't prove constant time, so rely on the standard library.
str | None, list[str], dict[str, int]. FastAPI and Pydantic use them to parse and validate requests, so you need to read them fluently.

checks.t: I can make a venv, install a package, and run a script that uses it
I can turn a list of user dicts into the names of the active ones with one comprehension
I can explain why def f(tags=[]) shares one list between calls
I can say how if not token: and if token is None: differ for an empty string
I can write a UTC-aware "is this cert expired?" check and say why naive breaks

plan.title: FastAPI from the first route, then async

items.t: First app: app = FastAPI() and one @app.get route
items.why: Run it with fastapi dev main.py and open /docs: FastAPI writes the interactive API docs from your type hints. Go through the tutorial pages in order.
Name in the path: path param. Simple type: query param. Pydantic model: body. A list[str] needs Query() or FastAPI reads it as the body.
Validate input with types and Field(...) limits. Use response_model so fields like password_hash never leak in responses.
Know when to return 401, 403, 404, 409, 422 and 502. A bad body gets 422 from Pydantic before your code runs. Interviewers notice a wrong status code.
FastAPI's dependency injection, like Laravel/Symfony DI. Used for auth checks, the current user, and the database session.

items.t: Build one: a small notes API
items.why: GET /notes, POST /notes, DELETE /notes/{id}, a Pydantic model, a dict in memory, 404 for a missing id. Try every route from /docs. Then read app.py behind this page: the same pieces with SQLite.

items.t: The event loop: one thread, switches only at await
items.why: Read this page first. It is the clearest explanation of async in Python.
Blocking: time.sleep, requests, sync database drivers. Non-blocking: asyncio.sleep, httpx.AsyncClient, async drivers. await requests.get(...) is a TypeError.
How to run several awaits at the same time, and why time.sleep inside them makes them run one after another.
async def runs on the event loop. Plain def runs in a threadpool (about 40 threads). If a handler must call blocking code, plain def is the safe choice.
Create shared things (an httpx.AsyncClient, the DB engine) once at startup and close them at shutdown.

checks.t: I can write a FastAPI route with a path param, a query param and a body without looking it up
I can explain why one blocking call slows down unrelated endpoints
I can give both fixes (async client, or plain def) and the trade-off
I know how FastAPI decides between path, query and body

items.t: When SQL actually runs: add, flush, autoflush, commit
items.why: Nothing is sent on add() or on setting an attribute. Flush sends it inside the transaction (ids appear, constraint errors fire); commit ends it. Closing without commit rolls back. Unlike Drupal's save(), which writes at once.

items.t: After commit objects reload; after close they can't (DetachedInstanceError)
items.why: expire_on_commit makes the next attribute read a fresh SELECT. A closed session can't do that, nor a lazy load like d.owner. Build the response while the session is open, refresh(), or expire_on_commit=False.

items.t: One session per request, via Depends() with yield
items.why: Never a module-level db = Session(engine): it is shared by every request and every thread.
After an error, the session must be rolled back. If not, every later use fails with "transaction has been rolled back due to a previous exception".
"Check if it exists, then insert" has a race: two requests both pass the check. Let the database enforce it.

items.t: Bound parameters, never f-strings in SQL
items.why: select(Device).where(Device.serial == serial) or text("... WHERE serial = :serial"). Same idea as PDO prepared statements.
Loading related rows in a loop runs one query per row. Use selectinload. List endpoints need a limit.
Filter by owner or tenant inside the query, not after loading. Your PHP experience transfers directly here.
Plain assert, fixtures, @pytest.mark.parametrize, monkeypatch.
Call endpoints in tests and swap the real database or auth for a test one.
Pass now in as a parameter. Fake upstreams at the transport (httpx.MockTransport). Don't depend on the machine's timezone or the network. Say what a test can't prove.

checks.t: I can explain why db = Session(engine) at module level breaks under load
I can write a test that registers the same serial twice and expects 409
I can say what a given test cannot prove

items.why: Ask an AI assistant or a friend for concept-first questions on what you covered, and answer out loud: the bug, the fix, the test. The drills tab has more than two dozen, very easy to moderate-hard; do any you haven't.
Two minutes on a project you built: what it does, the stack, one hard problem and how you solved it, and what you'd do differently. Expect follow-ups on each.
A rested head reasons better than one more hour of reading.
FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, pytest and the Python standard library. If docs are allowed, use them; looking things up well is part of the job.
Read the whole snippet first. Name the worst bug first, with a concrete example. Give the fix, then the test, then what the test can't prove. Then rank the other issues.

items.t: Know what to say when you're unsure
items.why: "In PHP I'd do X. I'd check the docs for the exact Python syntax, but the fix is Y." That shows judgement, which is what they score.
